name: Winston Churchill
info: Sir Winston Churchill was a British statesman, soldier and writer, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940 to 1945 and again from 1951 to 1955, remembered above all as Britain's leader in the Second World War.

facts.born: 30 November 1874, at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire; son of the Conservative politician Lord Randolph Churchill and Jennie, daughter of the American businessman Leonard Jerome, of the aristocratic Spencer family and a descendant of the 1st Duke of Marlborough
facts.died: 24 January 1965, at his London home, 28 Hyde Park Gate, after a final stroke on 10 January; given a state funeral and buried at St Martin's Church, Bladon
facts.role: Army officer and war correspondent (1895-1900); Member of Parliament for some 62 of the years between 1900 and 1964; President of the Board of Trade (1908-1910); Home Secretary (1910-1911); First Lord of the Admiralty (1911-1915, 1939-1940); Chancellor of the Exchequer (1924-1929); Prime Minister (1940-1945, 1951-1955); leader of the Conservative Party (1940-1955)
facts.known: Leading Britain through the Second World War; his wartime speeches; the Dardanelles campaign; social reforms as a Liberal minister; returning sterling to the gold standard; the "iron curtain" speech; the Nobel Prize in Literature (1953); his record in the Empire, from Iraq to the Bengal famine

t: Churchill was a soldier and war correspondent before entering Parliament in 1900, and he crossed from the Conservatives to the Liberals and back, holding most of the great offices of state over half a century.

As prime minister from May 1940 he refused to seek a peace settlement after the fall of France, led a coalition government and built the alliance with the United States and the Soviet Union that defeated Germany in 1945.

A staunch imperialist, he has been criticised for his views on race and for decisions such as the bombing of Iraq in the 1920s, his government's response to the Bengal famine and the area bombing of Germany.
dyk: Churchill had a lateral lisp from childhood and worked on his pronunciation of the letter 's'; he turned the impediment into an asset, as when he called Hitler a "Nar-zee".
ev: Winston Churchill is born at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire
He is elected Conservative MP for Oldham, aged 25, after his escape from a Boer prisoner-of-war camp
The naval attack on the Dardanelles and the Gallipoli campaign fail, and he is removed from the Admiralty
As Chancellor of the Exchequer he returns sterling to the gold standard
He becomes prime minister and resolves to fight on after the fall of France
Germany surrenders; weeks later the Conservatives lose the general election to Labour
He returns as prime minister, serving until his resignation in 1955
Churchill dies in London and is given a state funeral

sections.early:
Winston Leonard Spencer Churchill was born on 30 November 1874 at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, his family's ancestral home. Through his father, the Conservative MP Lord Randolph Churchill, he belonged to the aristocracy as a descendant of John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough; his mother, Jennie, was a daughter of the American businessman Leonard Jerome. For much of the 1880s his parents were effectively estranged, and he and his brother Jack were cared for by their nanny, Elizabeth Everest, whom he later called his "dearest and most intimate friend".

He was not academic and his behaviour was poor at his first boarding school, but he improved at Brunswick School in Hove and in 1888 entered Harrow, where his father had him prepare for the army. After two failed attempts he entered the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, as a cavalry cadet in 1893. His father died in January 1895.

Commissioned into the 4th Queen's Own Hussars in February 1895, he used his mother's influence to see action. He observed the Cuban War of Independence, served in India, where he read widely in Plato, Gibbon, Darwin and Macaulay, and joined the Malakand Field Force on the North West Frontier, the subject of his first book. In September 1898 he rode in one of the British Army's last cavalry charges, at Omdurman in the Sudan, and wrote The River War. He left the army, critical of Kitchener's unmerciful treatment of enemy wounded.
sections.rise:
He lost the Oldham by-election of June 1899 and went to the Second Boer War as a journalist for the Morning Post. Captured when Boer artillery derailed his train, he escaped from a prison camp in Pretoria in December and reached Portuguese East Africa, an escape that attracted much publicity. In October 1900 he was elected Conservative MP for Oldham, aged 25.

A free trader, he opposed the Conservatives' turn to protectionism, and in May 1904 he attacked the Aliens Bill, designed to curb Jewish immigration, for its "racial prejudice against Jews". On 31 May 1904 he crossed the floor to the Liberals, a defection that may have been influenced by ambition. Under Asquith he became President of the Board of Trade in 1908, the youngest Cabinet member since 1866, and with Lloyd George championed social reform: trade boards that established the principle of a minimum wage, labour exchanges and the National Insurance Act 1911, which he helped draft. In September 1908 he married Clementine Hozier, his wife until his death. As Home Secretary from 1910 he reformed the prisons and commuted 21 of 43 death sentences.

In October 1911 Asquith made him First Lord of the Admiralty. He built up the navy against Germany, encouraged naval aviation, coined the word "seaplane" and in 1914 secured for the government a 51% share in the profits of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company to supply the fleet.
sections.deeds:
After Germany invaded Norway, Churchill became prime minister on 10 May 1940, the day German forces attacked the Low Countries. He formed a war cabinet with Labour, made himself Minister of Defence and, at the end of May, overcame Lord Halifax's proposal to explore a peace settlement through Mussolini. His speeches, from "blood, toil, tears and sweat" to "we shall fight on the beaches" and "their finest hour", hardened opinion against a peaceful resolution; Roy Jenkins called them "an inspiration for the nation". Through the Battle of Britain and the Blitz he ordered the Special Operations Executive and the Commandos into being.

His good relations with Franklin D. Roosevelt helped secure supplies and, from 1941, Lend-Lease; in August 1941 they issued the Atlantic Charter. After Pearl Harbor he agreed with Roosevelt that Germany should be defeated first. He met Stalin in Moscow in 1942 and in the "Big Three" conferences at Tehran in 1943 and Yalta in 1945, and argued for invading Sicily and Italy before France. After the fall of Singapore in February 1942, which he called "the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British military history", the tide turned with El Alamein and Stalingrad. Allied forces landed in Normandy on 6 June 1944, and on 8 May 1945 he announced Germany's surrender.
sections.opponents:
Churchill's critics found much to fault. Many MPs held him responsible for the failure at the Dardanelles and Gallipoli in 1915. The labour movement long distrusted him after the Tonypandy riots of 1910 and his part in opposing the General Strike of 1926. As Chancellor he restored the gold standard in 1925 against the advice of economists including John Maynard Keynes, a move held to have caused deflation and unemployment. He supported the Black and Tans in Ireland, proposed equipping aircraft in Iraq with "poison gas" to punish "recalcitrant natives", which was never done, and as Colonial Secretary in 1921 pushed his plan for the aerial bombing of Iraq, which the Cabinet approved; the historian Yuki Tanaka sees that precedent as leading to indiscriminate bombing of Europeans in the Second World War. He called Gandhi "a seditious Middle Temple lawyer, now posing as a fakir".

In the Bengal famine of 1943, in which an estimated 2.1-3.8 million people died, his government was criticised for refusing more grain imports, which it ascribed to a shortage of shipping; the Viceroy, Lord Wavell, complained of "neglect, even sometimes with hostility and contempt", and the effect of British policy on the toll remains controversial. The area bombing he initiated killed about 24,000 at Dresden in February 1945; Max Hastings, quoted by Andrew Marr, called his later memo an attempt to distance himself from the controversy. According to Paul Addison he opposed immigration from the Commonwealth, and a 1910 letter shows support for eugenics.
sections.last:
With Labour leaving the coalition, Churchill led a caretaker government into the general election of July 1945. He mishandled the campaign, claiming in a broadcast that Labour would need "some form of Gestapo", and lost heavily to Clement Attlee. As Leader of the Opposition he warned in 1946 of an "iron curtain" across Europe, called for a special relationship with the United States and was an early advocate of European unity. Between his terms he wrote his six-volume memoir The Second World War, and in 1953 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature.

He returned as prime minister in October 1951, nearly 77 and in poor health. His government met Macmillan's target of 300,000 new houses a year, while abroad he sought to preserve what remained of the Empire, maintaining the military response in the Malayan Emergency and against the Mau Mau Uprising in Kenya, and seeking co-operation with the United States. He was knighted in 1953, and on 23 June that year suffered a serious stroke that was kept secret. He resigned on 5 April 1955 and was succeeded by Anthony Eden.

He declined a dukedom, stood down from the Commons in 1964 and spent his retirement at Chartwell, in London and on the French Riviera. In 1963 he was made an honorary citizen of the United States. He suffered his final stroke on 10 January 1965 and died at 28 Hyde Park Gate on 24 January. After lying in state at Westminster Hall he was given a state funeral at St Paul's Cathedral and buried at Bladon.
sections.legacy:
Churchill is regarded as one of the 20th century's most significant figures and remains popular in the United Kingdom, generally seen as a victorious wartime leader who helped defend liberal democracy against fascism. Historians rank him among the greatest British prime ministers, and in a 2002 BBC poll he was voted the greatest-ever Briton. Memorials include his statue in Parliament Square, the Churchill War Rooms and Churchill College, Cambridge. He was the first of only eight people granted honorary citizenship of the United States.

Before the Second World War his two changes of party bred widespread "mistrust and dislike", and some saw him as driven more by ambition than by principle; Robert Rhodes James found him "refreshingly innocent and straightforward". Biographers have called him "fundamentally conservative" and "liberal in outlook". Paul Addison describes the reformer as a "benevolent paternalist", and Jenkins credited him with "a substantial record as a social reformer". He was a staunch imperialist with a "romanticised view" of the Empire, and he has sometimes been criticised for his comments on race and for wartime decisions such as area bombing; Addison argues that he would never have tried "to stoke up racial animosity against immigrants".

He was a prolific writer of history, biography and memoir, including the four-volume A History of the English-Speaking Peoples, and an amateur painter of hundreds of canvases.

summary: Winston Churchill, born at Blenheim Palace in 1874, was a soldier and war correspondent, a Liberal and Conservative minister and twice prime minister. He led Britain through the Second World War from 1940, and is honoured as a wartime leader while criticised for his imperialism, his views on race and decisions from Iraq to the Bengal famine.
notes: Iraq: the article says that as Colonial Secretary (from February 1921) he pushed his plan for aerial bombing, 'Cabinet approved it in August and eight RAF squadrons were sent to Iraq the next year'; I gave the plan and its approval, not a date for the bombing.
Dresden: the article says the area bombing campaign was 'initiated by Churchill in January' 1945 and gives 'a death toll of about 24,000' from a 2010 commission.
'Lost heavily': the article calls the 1945 result a 'landslide Labour victory'.
'Many reasons have been given' for the 1945 defeat; I gave only the Gestapo broadcast, which Jenkins says had a significant bearing.
Marigold's birth: one passage says four days after the Armistice, the family section says November 1918; consistent, not used.

Wanted but not in the article: casualty figures for Gallipoli; numbers for the Mau Mau and Malayan campaigns; any account of Churchill's role in Operation Keelhaul beyond the Yalta agreement (left out).
